survey.title: Help us build AI for Founders
survey.intro: About ten minutes, and most of it is writing, not ticking. We are drafting a sixteen-week programme for founders whose business still runs through them, and before we decide who teaches what, we want to know whether we are teaching the right things. So this asks about your week before it asks about our outline, and it asks you to answer in your own words. Your answers go to the people writing the curriculum, not to a dashboard. Version two is published with the changes marked, so you can see what moved because of you.
survey.length: About 10 minutes · 20 questions · 12 open · answer the ones that speak to you
survey.method: The survey runs on Compassionate Curiosity, Kwame Christian's three-step frame for conversations where someone wants something: acknowledge and validate the feeling, get curious with compassion, then solve the problem together. Part one lets people name what the week feels like before we ask anything about us. Parts two to four ask open questions in a warm register, for stories and specifics rather than opinions. Part five turns the conversation into joint problem solving: what would need to be true in March, who should be in the room, and how far they want to go with us. People value what they help build, so the last part is the point, not an afterthought.

brief_map.how: Part one: who they are, what they sell, how many hours the business needs them, and a week told in their own words (questions 1 to 4).
Question 15, what would need to be true in March for sixteen weeks to have been worth it, and question 9, where the outline is exactly their problem and where it is not.
Questions 9 to 12 on the outline: what is exactly right, what is missing, where to go deeper, what to skip. Every answer is logged and the recurring ones become the version two change log.
Question 3 (the week), question 7 (what still goes through them and which to lift first) and the module need grid at question 8.

brief_map.ask: What they do not know they should know.
brief_map.how: Asked directly at question 16, and surfaced indirectly by questions 5 and 6, where the story of the last attempt shows the gap they cannot name.

Questions 13 and 14, open: who they have learned most from, inside Mindvalley or outside, what it is about how that person teaches, and who they would want in the room. No list of names, so nothing is promised and names we have not thought of can appear.

brief_map.ask: Serves marketing as well as curriculum.
brief_map.how: Question 9 and question 15 give the language for the summit and the sales page in the audience's own words; question 13 tells marketing which voices this audience already trusts; question 18 builds the founding circle list.

The five parts are programme-agnostic: your week, what you have tried, the outline, who you learn from, building it together. Swap the module list and the outline link and it runs for any Mastery. Jaideep's deeper quiz at summit registration stays separate; this one runs before, to the warm community.

sections.title: Part 1 · Your week
sections.lead: Before anything about us: where you are, and what it is like. Three quick ones, then one that takes a minute.

questions.text: Which describes you best right now?
options: Solo founder: coach, consultant, practitioner or creator. The business is me.
Founder with a team of up to ten
Founder with a team of more than ten
Planning to start a business in the next year
I lead inside someone else's company
questions.why: The one split that changes everything downstream. Solo founders and founders with a team feel the same problem differently, and every lab runs in two tracks because of it. Sets the wording of question 7.

questions.text: What does your business mainly sell?
questions.why: Decides which examples and skill packs we build first. A coach's company brain and an agency's company brain hold different things.

questions.text: Tell us about a recent week when everything came back to you. What happened, and how did you feel by Friday?
questions.why: The first real question names the feeling before we ask for anything. People cannot think about a curriculum while the frustration is unspoken; asked this way, the frustration becomes the data. The phrases here become the opening of the summit and the sales page.

questions.text: In a normal week, how many hours does your business need you personally to keep running?
questions.why: The before picture. The whole programme is measured against the founder load map, and this is the first rough reading of it across the community.

sections.title: Part 2 · What you have tried
sections.lead: No judgement here. We learn more from what went wrong than from what went right.

questions.text: Walk us through the last time you tried to hand something to AI, or to a person. What did you hope would happen, and what actually happened?
questions.why: A story, not an opinion. The gap between hoped and happened is the knowledge gap or the application gap, in their words. This is where we learn whether the problem is knowing what to do or getting it to stick.

questions.text: What has stopped you going further with AI in your business? Say it the way you would say it to a friend.
questions.why: The blocker, uncoded. Asking for the friend version lowers the guard and gets the real reason (trust, time, fear of sounding like a robot, a bad first try) rather than the respectable one.

questions.text: Which of these still have to go through you? Tick everything that applies, then tell us the one you would most like off your desk first.
options: Finding leads and following them up
Deciding what to build or sell next
questions.why: The eight options are the eight modules in plain words and in no particular order. The tick pattern weights the pillars by founder type; the one pick tests the module order. For solo founders the hiring line reads delegating to contractors or AI.

sections.title: Part 3 · The outline
sections.lead: Read the draft outline (shown here and linked) and tell us what you think. Nothing in it is fixed.

questions.text: For each of the eight modules, how much do you need it?
questions.why: The one quantitative read on the outline. A four-point scale with no midpoint, so everyone leans one way. The share answering need it or urgently becomes each module's need index, by founder type.

questions.text: Reading the outline, where did you think: that is exactly my problem? And where did you think: that is not how it is for me?
questions.why: Two-sided on purpose. The first half gives marketing the hooks in the audience's words; the second half tells the curriculum where a lesson is framed for someone else.

questions.text: What problem in your business is nowhere in this outline?
questions.why: The gap question, asked as a problem rather than a topic. Every answer is logged; the recurring ones become the change log in version two.

questions.text: Where would you want us to go deeper, and what would deeper look like for you?
questions.why: Depth, with a definition. Deeper means different things: more time, more hand-holding, a template, a live build on their business. The second half tells us which.

questions.text: What would you skip, and why?
questions.why: Permission to cut. Sixteen weeks is long; the why separates already handled from do not believe it works.

sections.title: Part 4 · Who you learn from
sections.lead: Two questions about people. No names are promised; we want to understand what works for you.

questions.text: Who have you learned the most from about running a business, with AI or without, inside Mindvalley or outside? What is it about how they teach that works for you?
questions.why: Vishen's which teachers question, asked open. Names tell marketing which voices this audience already trusts; the second half tells the curriculum what teaching style to brief every guest on. Open, not a list, so nobody is promised and names we have not thought of can surface.

questions.text: Is there anyone you would want in the room for this programme? Tell us who, and why them.
questions.why: A wish list, framed as a question rather than a vote. The why matters more than the name: it tells us what the person represents (proof, warmth, a method) so we can look for it in whoever we confirm.

sections.title: Part 5 · Building it together
sections.lead: Now the part that makes this a conversation rather than a form.

questions.text: If we built this together, what would need to be true in March for you to say the sixteen weeks were worth it?
questions.why: The promise, in their words and their timeframe. We promise hours back, every lead answered and a business designed around AI; this tells us whether that is what they are buying, and the phrases become the sales page.

questions.text: What do you suspect you do not know yet, that a founder running on AI should know?
questions.why: Vishen's what they do not know they should know, asked directly. Answers here are the unprogrammed worries, the ones the quiz could not reach because nobody can tick a box for a thing they cannot name.

questions.text: How will you most likely take part, and which live times could you make?
options: Live when I can, recordings otherwise
questions.why: Availability, not a promise. The slot is set at 7am Pacific for team capacity; attendance data from five Masteries says the hour does not move turnout. This tells us how many will be live and how many will watch back, which shapes the labs.

questions.text: Would you like to be part of the founding circle that shapes version two?
options: Review version two before it is published
Test one system in my own business and report back
Share my founder load map, anonymised, as an example
Be quoted, first name and business type, in the curriculum
Join a 45-minute group call with the curriculum team
Not this time, just keep me posted
questions.why: The commitment question. Everyone who ticks anything but the last option has put something in, and the list becomes the founding circle: the people most likely to enrol and most likely to tell others.

questions.text: Anything else you want the people building this to know?
questions.why: The door left open. The most useful answer in a survey is often to the question nobody asked.

questions.text: May we follow up with you on your answers?
questions.type: Yes or no, with email pre-filled
options: No, use my answers but do not contact me about them
questions.why: Consent, and the join to the quiz and summit records. Pre-filling the email from the campaign link removes the one field that costs completions.

survey.thanks: Thank you. Your answers go straight to the people writing the curriculum, and they are read in full. Version two of the outline is published on [date], with every change marked, so you can see what moved because of you. If you asked to join the founding circle you will hear from us within a week. The AI for Founders Summit runs 30 October to 1 November; your seat is saved at [link].
design_notes: Length: about ten minutes. Twenty questions, twelve of them open; ten required. The intro says answer the ones that speak to you, so a half-finished survey still gives us parts one and two.

Order follows Compassionate Curiosity: acknowledge (part 1), get curious (parts 2 to 4), build together (part 5). The feeling is asked for before any opinion about us; the commitment comes last, once they have already invested.

Open questions ask for a story or a specific, never a rating in words: a recent week, the last time you tried, what would deeper look like, what would need to be true in March. Specifics are quotable; opinions are not.
Closed questions do two jobs only: segment (1, 2, 4) and give one quantitative read on the outline (7, 8). Everything else is written in their words.
No leading wording, no agree/disagree statements, one idea per question. The four-point scale has no midpoint.
Branching: question 1 sets the wording of question 7. The outline is shown inline before question 8 so nobody leaves the form.
Incentive is recognition, not a prize: early sight of version two, a named place in the thank-you section, the founding circle.
Send on a Tuesday, remind on Friday, close the following Tuesday. One reminder, to non-openers and partial completions only.
Mobile first, progress shown, email pre-filled from the campaign link. Typeform or an Airtable form; responses land in the AI for Founders base once Vishen has aligned, in a sheet until then.
analysis: Segment every answer by founder type (question 1) and what they sell (question 2). The draft already runs two tracks; this tells us whether two is enough.

Open answers are read in full, not summarised. Questions 3, 5, 6, 9, 15 and 16 are coded by hand into recurring themes; the phrases themselves go into a language bank for lesson copy and the sales page.
Module need index: the share answering need it or need it urgently on question 8, by segment, read against question 7 to test the module order.
Gaps and depth: questions 10 to 12 become the version two change log, with a rough count beside each change.
Teachers: questions 13 and 14 produce two lists, names and teaching qualities. The qualities brief every guest; the names go to the summit and Mastery roster conversation, not to the page.
Format: question 17 sets lab design and tells us the live-to-recording split to plan for.
Founding circle: everyone who ticks an active option in question 18 goes on a list with their answers attached. They see version two first.
Version two is published with a change log that credits the survey: what moved, and roughly how many people asked for it.

emails.body:
Hi [Name],

Expert & Authority Mastery sold out.

I want to say thank you before anything else. You came to the summit, you asked hard questions in the Q&A, you told us what you were building and what was in the way. The programme that's running right now was shaped by that. The curriculum came out of your survey answers before a single lesson was written. That's the only way I know how to build.

So here's what's next.

On 30 October to 1 November we're running a new, free, three-day event: the AI for Founders Summit.

It's not about learning AI. We already have a programme for that. This one is about the business. Specifically, the founder's problem nobody teaches: everything still runs through you. Every lead, every proposal, every client question, every decision waits for your hours. You built the business to be free and somewhere along the way it took the freedom. [Vishen: your own Mindvalley example here, two sentences, the one from the story interview.]

Over three days we'll show you what to automate first in your business, then build it live, step by step. The company brain. The lead that never goes cold. Content in your own voice.

Here's where you come in.

Back in 2015 we built a programme with our community instead of for it. We shared the rough outline, asked what was missing, and published the version they'd shaped. It was the best launch we'd ever done, and the programme was better for it.

I want to do that again. This week you'll get a short survey from us: where your business is, what eats your week, what you'd want a programme like this to fix first. Then we'll publish the curriculum for the summit and the Mastery, openly, before it's finished, and ask you what's missing.

[Photo: Vishen and Gareth, MVU or the KL office. Working, not posed. Group shot with Jaideep if one exists.]

The person reading your answers is Gareth Winter, our Head of Content and Creative Director. Gareth designs our curricula. He'll take what you tell us and publish version two of the programme with your input in it, so you can see exactly what changed because of you.

Save your seat here, and watch for the survey.

[Link: save my seat at the AI for Founders Summit]

Vishen

P.S. from Gareth: I read every answer, not a summary of them. The questions you asked in the Expert & Authority survey are already in this curriculum. Tell me what's missing, and you'll see it in the next version. Gareth

Register: no exclamation marks, no formal connectives, one coined idea (co-create) used three times; the enemy is the inherited setup of the business, never the reader. Role credit for consistent use: Gareth Winter, Head of Content and Creative Director, designs Mindvalley's curricula.

modules.name: Module 1: Strategy: find the bottleneck
modules.installed: Founder load map; an audit that ranks where AI pays off; a 90-day roadmap.
modules.changes: The founder knows the three workflows to fix first, and which to keep human.

modules.name: Module 2: Company brain
modules.problem: AI gives generic answers; the team keeps asking the founder.
modules.installed: Shared context, offers, customers, voice, processes and decisions, in one place the whole team uses.
modules.changes: Every later system, and every team member, works from one source.

modules.name: Module 3: Marketing
modules.problem: Content depends on the founder's time.
modules.installed: Voice-trained content skills: one idea into a week of posts, emails and pages.
modules.changes: Consistent output without the founder writing each piece.

modules.name: Module 4: Sales
modules.installed: Lead research, qualification, follow-up and proposal skills; call prep and debrief.
modules.changes: Every lead answered and followed up; the founder takes only the calls that need them.

modules.name: Module 5: Operations and delivery
modules.problem: Client work and questions land on the founder.
modules.installed: Client onboarding flow; processes turned into skills; first-line support drafts; scheduled check-ins.
modules.changes: Routine client work runs from the system; the founder reviews rather than does.

modules.name: Module 6: Team: people and AI
modules.installed: AI team members per role; hiring, onboarding and training kits; delegation briefs.
modules.changes: Solo: contractors plus AI instead of a first hire. Team: new people productive in days.

modules.name: Module 7: Finance and the founder's cockpit
modules.problem: The numbers arrive too late to act on.
modules.installed: Weekly business dashboard; expense and invoice triage; decision memos.
modules.changes: One weekly view the founder decides from.

modules.name: Module 8: Product and scale
modules.problem: What to build or sell next.
modules.installed: Offer and pricing research; the weekly operating rhythm; an AI-first org chart.
modules.changes: A company designed around AI, not AI bolted onto the old one.

notes: Rebuilt on 5 October from three sources: Vykintas Glodenis’s curriculum proposal (eight modules, one business pillar each, the problem / management idea / installed system / observable change pattern, and the Get AI-Ready onboarding layer), Jaideep’s launch brief (16 weeks from Monday 16 November, two sessions per module, the summit on 30 October to 1 November), and the AI for Founders quiz (812 answers: operations, marketing and sales are where the pain is; solo founders start with marketing, founders with teams with operations; data safety and sounding like me are the unprogrammed worries).

Team direction, 26 September (Jaideep, Marijana, Marta): Vishen leads the summit and takes only the big Mastery sessions; Vykintas leads the Mastery curriculum and every implementation lab; roughly one guest teacher per pillar; at least one more woman on the roster. Every guest here is placed where they are most authentic, from the names in consideration on 5 October, and none is confirmed for the Mastery until the team says so.

Cadence, decided 5 October, hour set 7 October: Tuesday lesson, Thursday lab, 7am Pacific (3pm London; 2pm London in the final week), Tuesday 17 November 2026 to Thursday 18 March 2027, with a break from 21 December to 3 January. Expert & Authority runs Tuesday and Friday; this programme deliberately does not match it. Vykintas leads every lab here and already holds 8 of Expert & Authority’s Friday workshops at 9am Pacific inside this run (20 Nov, 27 Nov, 18 Dec, 8 Jan, 29 Jan, 5 Feb, 12 Feb, 19 Feb), so a Friday lab would put him in two rooms on the same morning on each of those dates.

The opening is Monday 16 November, the start date in the brief, with Vishen. It also keeps him clear of his Expert & Authority lesson at the same hour on Tuesday 17 November once the John Lee rotation is applied.

Thanksgiving, decided 5 October and checked against the day on 7 October: the Week 2 lab stays on Thursday 26 November, Thanksgiving Day in the US. Expert & Authority’s 2025 reading was that the week holds, and it kept its Friday 27 November workshop. The 2025 Mastery records confirm the week and sharpen the day: AI Mastery’s sessions the day before (422 against 454 and 447 the Wednesdays either side) and the day after (307 against 274 and 313) showed no dip; the one session that ran on Thanksgiving Day itself, Entrepreneurship Mastery’s Thursday lesson, kept 214 of a usual 300, about 70 percent, and its recording was watched more that week than any other Thursday’s that month. So the lab runs, Vykintas-led and recorded, and the Tuesday 1 December lesson picks up anyone who missed it. Wednesday 25 November is the alternative if the team prefers not to run on the day; the day before showed no dip.

Time slot, set 7 October: 7am Pacific, which is 3pm London for every week but the last and 2pm London on 16 and 18 March 2027 (US clocks change on 14 March, UK clocks on 28 March). Janja set the hour for team capacity and schedule; the data supports it. Attendance across five Mastery bases shows no hour effect between 7am and 10am Pacific (Entrepreneurship Mastery moved from 5pm to 3pm London mid-cohort and attendance did not move), Manifesting and Speaking & Influence Mastery run at 3pm London with the highest live rates in the set, and the final hour-by-hour preference was for 9am because about 60 percent of students are in North America; that was never a hill to die on. Students are told the Pacific time; London is the derived time. Evidence in briefs/AIF-TIME-SLOT-EVIDENCE.md.

What this programme leaves to AI Mastery: how models work, prompting in depth, image and video generation, writing skills from scratch, building apps. Where both touch the same tool the angle differs: the brain in AI Mastery is your personal knowledge; here it is the company’s, shared with the team. Neither is the advanced one.

Outside the modules there are only three sessions, all before Week 1: Get AI-Ready calls 1 and 2, which are Vykintas’s and in his proposal as written (the content of each call is a first pass), and the Monday opening with Vishen, the kickoff from the earlier draft moved to the start date in the brief. Office hours and an alumni reunion were in the earlier draft and were removed on 7 October: Vishen’s diary cannot carry extra calls, and what happens after graduation is a separate conversation, not part of the Mastery. Expert & Authority’s own Airtable holds only lessons, workshops, one bonus and the graduation.

Summit learnings applied: a live build directly before every offer; every session leaves something built; written topic lock for every Vishen session two weeks ahead and no previews of unreleased tools; a sound check at every speaker handoff; untested builders get a paid webinar or Highlights slot before the summit; Shawn never follows Vykintas in the same event.

sessions.title: Get AI-Ready, call 1: your account, your first project, your first skill
sessions.description:
Call 1, the first week after the summit, for early buyers: the building blocks walked live, questions answered, the checklist started. Recorded for late buyers.

Get AI-Ready: the shared floor before Week 1. Three layers, so no live lesson ever has to teach setup: optional pre-recorded base setup for founders starting from zero (signing up, which plan, starting a chat, adding files, voice, and a short guide for people coming from ChatGPT); required building blocks for everyone (prompt and context, skills, projects and instructions, connectors, scheduled tasks, cloud versus local), each with one thing set up in your own account; then the programme. The readiness checklist nudges, it does not gate: a paid plan, one project with instructions, one skill installed, one app connected. It also gives us the starting-level data the AI Mastery 2026 survey was missing.

sessions.title: Get AI-Ready, call 2: checklist, connectors and the questions from call 1
sessions.description:
Call 2, the week before the start, for late buyers who watched the recording of call 1 and for anyone still stuck on setup. Nobody arrives at Week 1 wondering what a connector is.

Get AI-Ready: the shared floor before Week 1. Three layers, so no live lesson ever has to teach setup: optional pre-recorded base setup for founders starting from zero (signing up, which plan, starting a chat, adding files, voice, and a short guide for people coming from ChatGPT); required building blocks for everyone (prompt and context, skills, projects and instructions, connectors, scheduled tasks, cloud versus local), each with one thing set up in your own account; then the programme. The readiness checklist nudges, it does not gate: a paid plan, one project with instructions, one skill installed, one app connected. It also gives us the starting-level data the AI Mastery 2026 survey was missing.

sessions.title: Why Your Business Still Runs on You
sessions.description: The programme opens on Monday 16 November with Vishen. You built the business to be free; somewhere along the way it took the freedom. Vishen opens his own load map live: the years Mindvalley ran through him, and what AI runs there today. Then the ceiling every founder in the room shares: your business cannot grow faster than your calendar. Vykintas walks the sixteen weeks, the teacher on each, and the one measurement graduation is judged against: how many hours a week your business needs you today. You leave with the calendar in your hands and a number written down.

sessions.title: Your Founder Load Map
sessions.description: Where do your hours actually go? The load map is the instrument the whole programme is measured against: every lead, proposal, client question and decision that waits for you, logged for one week. Vykintas teaches how to read it, how to rank each workflow by what AI would give back, and the test for what stays human. This is also the before picture: how many hours a week your business needs you today.
sessions.brief: Where your hours actually go. One week of every lead, proposal, client question and decision that waits for you, logged and ranked by what AI would give back, with a test for what should stay human. The before picture the whole programme is measured against.

sessions.title: Map the Week, Rank the Leverage
sessions.description:
Load map filled in on your real week, in the two tracks the quiz showed: solo founders start with content and leads, founders with a team start with the approvals and admin that reach them. Three workflows named, one chosen.

**The win:** You know what to automate first, and it is written down

sessions.title: What to Hand to AI First
sessions.description: Nate was a spreadsheet analyst with no coding background; within a year he ran an AI agency serving brands like Topgolf and BarkBox. Most founders try to automate everything at once and stall. He teaches how AI-native founders think instead: start with the few workflows that quietly drain a small team every week, hand those over, and only then widen. The management idea for the whole programme: AI first, then people for what only people do.
sessions.brief: Why founders who try to automate everything at once stall, and how AI-native founders think instead: hand over the few workflows that quietly drain a small team every week, then widen. AI first, then people for what only people do.

sessions.title: Your 90-Day Roadmap
sessions.description:
The roadmap built against your load map: which pillar first, which system each month, what success looks like at module 8. The first workflow from the map handed over before the lab ends. The lab falls on US Thanksgiving and runs as scheduled; it is recorded.

**The win:** A dated plan, and one job already off your desk
sessions.note: Thanksgiving Day in the US. The lab runs as scheduled and is recorded; the Week 3 lesson on Tuesday 1 December picks up anyone who misses it.

sessions.title: The Company Brain
sessions.description: From a personal AI memory to the company's: mission, offers, customers, voice, numbers, processes and the decisions you have already made, in one governed place every tool and every team member reads. Record-everything as an organisation, not a habit. Vykintas teaches the brain every pillar after this one runs on, then builds it with you two days later.
sessions.brief: From a personal AI memory to the company’s: mission, offers, customers, voice, numbers, processes and the decisions already made, in one governed place every tool and every team member reads.

sessions.title: Stand Up Your Company Brain
sessions.description:
Offers, voice, customers, numbers and proof stories loaded into a governed project. Interrogated against your real numbers until it answers like someone who works there.

**The win:** An AI that answers like your co-founder, by Thursday night

sessions.title: What Goes In, and What Never Does
sessions.description: Data safety was the question the $100K+ founders in the quiz asked most. Noelle brings enterprise AI governance sized for a three-person company: which model and tools, who can see what, where client information never goes, and the human checkpoint that keeps trust. The management idea is simple: a brain the team uses has to be a brain you would show a lawyer.
sessions.brief: Data safety for a small company: which models and tools, who can see what, where client information never goes, and the human checkpoint that keeps trust. A brain the team uses has to be one you would show a lawyer.

sessions.title: Feed the Brain, Safely
sessions.description:
Document and meeting pipelines wired in so the brain stays current without you. An AI policy for your business written and adopted. A blind-spot report generated from your own data.

**The win:** A brain your whole team uses, and your AI spots a problem you had missed

sessions.title: The One-Person Marketing Team
sessions.description: Sabrina sold her first AI company, then grew to more than three million followers in 24 months with no funding, no ads and no team. She teaches how one person now matches the output of a twenty-person marketing team with agents, what she still does herself, and what she never hands over. Content is the solo founder's biggest time-eater in the quiz, and this is the week it stops being one.
sessions.brief: How one person now matches the output of a large marketing team with agents, what still gets done by hand, and what never gets handed over. The week content stops eating the founder’s time.

sessions.title: Your Voice, Made Executable
sessions.description:
A voice skill trained on your own words, not a template. One idea turned into a week of posts, emails and a page, with an anti-slop gate so nothing ships that sounds like AI. The answer to the quiz's most repeated worry: sounding like me.

**The win:** Content that sounds like you, on demand

sessions.title: From Content to a List
sessions.description: Content that nobody captures is a hobby. Ruben built EasyGen and grew a founder audience on LinkedIn with AI doing the drafting; he teaches the distribution layer: which platform is your front door, how AI turns attention into a list, and the signals that tell you demand is real before you sell. Marketing's second half: not more content, a list that grows while you work.
sessions.brief: Content nobody captures is a hobby. Which platform is your front door, how AI turns attention into a list, and the signals that tell you demand is real before you sell.

sessions.title: Your Lead-Capture Asset, Live
sessions.description:
An assessment or scorecard built and shipped in-session, wired to the brain, with a signal dashboard counting real interest by the end of the lab.

**The win:** A lead machine with your name on it, on the internet

sessions.title: The Lead That Never Goes Cold
sessions.description: Firms that answer a lead within an hour are about seven times more likely to qualify it. Liam builds these systems inside real small businesses every week: research the lead, qualify it, reply in the founder's voice, book the call. He teaches where automation lifts conversion and the exact moments where it kills trust and a human has to step in.
sessions.brief: Answering a lead within the hour changes whether it converts. Research, qualification, a reply in your voice and a booked call, with the exact moments where automation would kill trust and a human steps in.

sessions.title: The Follow-Up Engine
sessions.description:
Lead research and qualification skills installed; follow-up sequences running from your CRM or inbox; every new lead answered within the hour with a human checkpoint before anything is promised.

**The win:** No lead goes cold in your business again

sessions.title: Outbound on Autopilot
sessions.description: Finding the next client is the job most founders still do alone. Nick builds outbound and lead systems for a living: AI finds the right prospects, writes to them one by one, and books the calls, so the pipeline keeps filling while the founder delivers. The management idea: sales as a system the founder reviews, not a task the founder performs.
sessions.brief: Finding the next client is the job most founders still do alone. AI finds the right prospects, writes to them one by one and books the calls, so the pipeline fills while you deliver. Sales as a system you review, not a task you perform.

sessions.title: Proposals, Call Prep and the Pipeline Cockpit
sessions.description:
Proposal generation from the brain; call prep and debrief skills; a pipeline view that shows which conversations need you this week and which the system is already handling.

**The win:** You take only the calls that need you

sessions.title: Delivery Agents and the Customer Experience
sessions.description: One agent, one job. Noelle walks through one founder's delivery running on AI end to end: onboarding, fulfilment support, service workflows, each handed to AI and each with the human checkpoint kept where trust lives. The management idea: clients should get the good version of your business whether or not you are in the room.
sessions.brief: One agent, one job. A founder’s delivery running on AI end to end: onboarding, fulfilment support and service workflows, each with the human checkpoint kept where trust lives. Clients get the good version of your business whether or not you are in the room.

sessions.title: Client Onboarding, Automated
sessions.description:
Your onboarding flow built end to end: welcome, intake, first-line support drafts, scheduled check-ins, escalation to you only where it should. Experience score instrumented.

**The win:** Delivery that scales without headcount

sessions.title: The Operations Brain
sessions.description: SOPs become skills. Meetings become operations data. Nate teaches the orchestration layer founders skip: scheduled runs, multi-step automations, the admin that eats evenings (inbox, invoices, scheduling) handed over with a review step. Operations was the pillar the quiz's team founders wanted fixed first; this is where it is.
sessions.brief: Standard procedures become skills, meetings become operations data. The orchestration layer founders skip: scheduled runs, multi-step automations, and the admin that eats evenings (inbox, invoices, scheduling) handed over with a review step.

sessions.title: Two Ops Automations, Live
sessions.description:
A reporting automation and an admin automation running on schedule before the lab ends, each with a checkpoint that lands in your inbox, not a task that lands on your desk.

**The win:** Monday starts with a report, not a scramble

sessions.title: Hiring Your First AI Employees
sessions.description: Callan runs 150 AI employees alongside a thirty-person human team, with nobody let go. She teaches the question every growing founder hits once the systems exist: who runs them? Which roles get an AI teammate first, which stay human, and for the solo founder the real version of the question: me, a contractor, or AI?
sessions.brief: Once the systems exist, who runs them? Which roles get an AI teammate first, which stay human, and for the solo founder the real question: me, a contractor, or AI?

sessions.title: Your First AI Team Member
sessions.description:
A role-to-agent pairing map for your business. One AI team member put into production with a delegation brief, a job description and a review rhythm, the way you would onboard a person.

**The win:** A job you no longer do, with a name on it

sessions.title: How Mindvalley's Team Works With Agents
sessions.description: Mindvalley's COO and CHRO, and author of Replaced by AI, on the org chart after AI: where agents now sit beside people, what one person does today that took three, and how to bring the humans with you so the team asks for more AI rather than less. Adoption and role redesign, from someone who has run it inside a company this size.
sessions.brief: The org chart after AI, from inside a company that has done it: where agents sit beside people, what one person does today that took three, and how to bring the humans with you so the team asks for more AI, not less.

sessions.title: The Hiring and Onboarding Kit
sessions.description:
Hiring, onboarding and training kits generated from the brain; an adoption scorecard; delegation briefs for your real team or your first future hire. Alex works the floor on the people questions.

**The win:** A new person productive in days, not months

sessions.title: The Finance Cockpit
sessions.module: Module 7: Finance and the founder's cockpit
sessions.description: Founder finance with AI: cashflow visibility, pricing and unit economics, forecasts, the weekly brief. The pillar every other programme skips, taught by a CPA with a Deloitte background so it is credible rather than aspirational. The management idea: decide from numbers that arrive on Monday, not from the accountant's summary in April.
sessions.brief: Founder finance with AI: cashflow visibility, pricing and unit economics, forecasts and a weekly brief. Decide from numbers that arrive on Monday, not from the accountant’s summary in April.

sessions.title: The Money Dashboard
sessions.module: Module 7: Finance and the founder's cockpit
sessions.description:
Cash, margin and forecast on one page, fed by the brain. Expense and invoice triage running on schedule. Scenario models for the next two decisions you are putting off.

**The win:** You stop flying blind on money

sessions.title: The Orchestrator's Week
sessions.module: Module 7: Finance and the founder's cockpit
sessions.description: Vishen's own operating system as a founder: the weekly brief he reads, the decision memos the team sends instead of meetings, how priorities, energy and focus get managed when the systems run and you lead. The week of an orchestrator, taught by the person the programme is modelled on.
sessions.brief: The week of a founder whose systems run: the weekly brief, decision memos instead of meetings, and how priorities, energy and focus are managed when you lead rather than do.

sessions.title: The Founder Cockpit
sessions.module: Module 7: Finance and the founder's cockpit
sessions.description:
One dashboard: pipeline, delivery health, money, the weekly AI founder brief and a priorities agent. Everything built since Week 3, read in one place.

**The win:** A business you can read in five minutes

sessions.title: The Founder Operating Rhythm
sessions.description: Matt built Founder OS on exactly this question: what to build or sell next, and the repeatable week that gets it shipped. Offer and pricing research run through the brain, the weekly operating rhythm that replaces heroics, and how a founder designs the company around the systems rather than around themselves.
sessions.brief: What to build or sell next, and the repeatable week that gets it shipped. Offer and pricing research through the brain, an operating rhythm that replaces heroics, and a company designed around the systems rather than around you.

sessions.title: Your Next Offer, Researched and Priced
sessions.description:
Offer and pricing research run against your customers and market; your weekly operating rhythm loaded into the cockpit; your AI-first org chart drawn: which work sits with people, which with agents, and what you hire next.

**The win:** You know what you are selling next, and who or what delivers it

sessions.brief: The load map from Week 1 measured again: the hours the business needs you now against then. The next twelve months designed, and certification on your Founder Operating System running in your business.
